title: Thermodynamics & ATP
outcomes: Laws of thermodynamics in living systems
Standard free energy and the equilibrium constant
Actual free energy in the cell
ATP, phosphoryl transfer and coupled reactions

summary.overview: Cells obey the laws of thermodynamics. Whether a reaction can proceed is decided by its actual free-energy change, ΔG, which depends on ΔG′° and on real concentrations. Unfavourable reactions are made to happen by coupling them to the hydrolysis of energy-rich molecules such as ATP.

sections.heading: Laws of thermodynamics
points: 1st law: energy is conserved. It can be transformed from one form to another but not created or destroyed.
2nd law: the entropy of the universe always increases.
Cells are open systems that exchange matter and energy with their surroundings and are never at equilibrium with them (e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ gradients).
Cells create internal order by releasing heat and increasing entropy in their surroundings, so the 2nd law is not violated.

sections.heading: Free energy
points: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. G is the free energy available to do work, H is the heat content (enthalpy) and S is disorder (entropy).
Negative ΔG: exergonic and spontaneous. Positive ΔG: endergonic, so it needs an energy input.
Thermodynamically favourable is not the same as fast. Glucose + O2 (ΔG′° = −2840 kJ/mol) is stable until enzymes lower the activation barrier.

sections.heading: ΔG′° and K′eq
points: ΔG′° is measured at 25 °C, pH 7, with all reactants and products at 1 M.
ΔG′° = −RT ln K′eq: K′eq > 1 gives a negative ΔG′°, K′eq = 1 gives zero, and K′eq < 1 gives a positive value.
At 25 °C, each 10-fold increase in K′eq makes ΔG′° about 5.7 kJ/mol more negative.
Example: phosphoglucomutase reaches 19 mM G6P and 1 mM G1P at equilibrium, so K′eq = 19 and ΔG′° ≈ −7.3 kJ/mol.

sections.heading: Actual ΔG in the cell
points: ΔG = ΔG′° + RT ln Q, where Q is the mass-action ratio of the actual concentrations.
It is ΔG, not ΔG′°, that decides direction: a reaction with a positive ΔG′° can proceed if products are kept low.
Cellular ATP is kept far above equilibrium, so the actual ΔG of ATP hydrolysis (about −50 to −65 kJ/mol) is much more negative than ΔG′° (−30.5 kJ/mol).

sections.heading: ATP and coupling
points: ATP hydrolysis is favourable because it relieves charge repulsion, and the products are better solvated and resonance-stabilised.
ΔG′° values are additive. Glucose + Pi → G6P (+13.8) plus ATP → ADP + Pi (−30.5) gives an overall −16.7 kJ/mol.
Phosphoryl groups flow from compounds with a more negative ΔG′° of hydrolysis to those with a less negative one: PEP (−61.9) and 1,3-BPG (−49.3) can make ATP; glucose 6-phosphate (−13.8) cannot.
Phosphocreatine (−43.0) buffers ATP in muscle via creatine kinase. Thioesters such as acetyl-CoA are also high-energy acyl donors.

keyTerms.definition: Energy available to do work at constant temperature and pressure.
Standard free-energy change at pH 7, 25 °C and 1 M concentrations; equal to −RT ln K′eq.
[products]/[reactants] at the actual concentrations in the cell.
Reaction with a negative ΔG that releases free energy.
Driving an endergonic reaction with an exergonic one through a shared intermediate.
Tendency of a compound to donate a phosphoryl group (more negative ΔG′° of hydrolysis = higher potential).

examTips: ΔG decides direction in the cell, not ΔG′°.
K′eq > 1 ⇔ ΔG′° negative; each factor of 10 ≈ 5.7 kJ/mol at 25 °C.
Favourable does not mean fast: rate depends on the activation barrier (ΔG‡).
Coupled reactions: just add the ΔG′° values of the two steps.

questions.outcome: Laws of thermodynamics in living systems
questions.stem: A growing calf builds highly ordered tissues. How is this consistent with the second law of thermodynamics?

options.text: The calf releases heat and simpler, higher-entropy products, so the entropy of the universe still rises
options.why: The 2nd law applies to system plus surroundings; local order is paid for by greater disorder elsewhere.

options.text: Living organisms are exempt from the second law, because their enzymes can reverse the flow of entropy
options.why: The laws of thermodynamics apply to all living systems.

options.text: The calf creates new energy from its food, and this extra energy is used to build order in its tissues
options.why: The 1st law forbids creating energy; it is only transformed.

options.text: The calf is a closed system at equilibrium with its environment, so its entropy does not need to change
options.why: Organisms are open systems that are never at equilibrium with their surroundings.

questions.outcome: Laws of thermodynamics in living systems
questions.stem: Why are living cells described as open thermodynamic systems?

options.text: They exchange both matter and energy with their surroundings
options.why: Cells take in nutrients and O2, release wastes and heat, and are never at equilibrium with their environment.

options.text: They exchange energy with their surroundings but not matter
options.why: That describes a closed system.

options.text: They exchange neither matter nor energy with their surroundings
options.why: That describes an isolated system.

options.text: They are kept at chemical equilibrium with their surroundings
options.why: Being at equilibrium would mean death: no gradients and no net flux.

questions.stem: Using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, which combination always gives a spontaneous (exergonic) process at any temperature?

options.text: ΔH negative and ΔS positive
options.why: Both terms then make ΔG negative regardless of T.

options.text: ΔH positive and ΔS negative
options.why: Both terms then make ΔG positive at every temperature.

options.text: ΔH positive and ΔS positive
options.why: This is spontaneous only when TΔS exceeds ΔH, i.e. at high enough temperature.

options.text: ΔH negative and ΔS negative
options.why: This is spontaneous only at low enough temperature.

questions.stem: The oxidation of glucose by O2 has ΔG′° = −2840 kJ/mol, yet sugar can sit in air for years without burning. Why?

options.text: It has a high activation barrier (ΔG‡); being thermodynamically favourable does not make it fast
options.why: ΔG decides whether a reaction can go; ΔG‡ decides how fast. Enzymes lower ΔG‡ so cells oxidise glucose step by step.

options.text: The reaction is actually endergonic in air, because the O2 concentration there is too low to drive it
options.why: A ΔG′° of −2840 kJ/mol is strongly exergonic.

options.text: Air contains no free oxygen at room temperature; O2 forms only once the sugar has been heated
options.why: Air is about 21% O2.

options.text: K′eq for glucose oxidation is less than 1, so at equilibrium most of the glucose remains intact
options.why: A very negative ΔG′° means a very large K′eq.

questions.outcome: Standard free energy and the equilibrium constant
questions.stem: A reaction has K′eq = 0.01. Starting with all components at 1 M, which way will it proceed?

options.text: In reverse, because ΔG′° is positive
options.why: K′eq < 1 means ΔG′° = −RT ln K′eq > 0, so under standard conditions the reverse reaction is favoured.

options.text: Forward, because ΔG′° is negative
options.why: A negative ΔG′° requires K′eq > 1.

options.text: It is already at equilibrium
options.why: Only K′eq = 1 means standard conditions are already equilibrium.

options.text: It cannot proceed in either direction
options.why: It moves in reverse until it reaches its equilibrium ratio.

questions.outcome: Standard free energy and the equilibrium constant
questions.stem: Phosphoglucomutase is given 20 mM glucose 1-phosphate. At equilibrium there is 1 mM G1P and 19 mM G6P. What is ΔG′° (R = 8.315 J/mol·K, T = 298 K)?

options.text: About −7.3 kJ/mol
About +7.3 kJ/mol
options.why: Products are favoured (K′eq > 1), so the sign must be negative.

options.text: About −3.2 kJ/mol
options.why: This uses log₁₀ instead of ln. With log₁₀ you must multiply by 2.303: ΔG′° = −2.303 RT log K′eq.

options.text: 0 kJ/mol, because the system is at equilibrium
options.why: ΔG = 0 at equilibrium, but ΔG′° is a constant calculated from K′eq.

questions.outcome: Standard free energy and the equilibrium constant
questions.stem: At 25 °C, a reaction has K′eq = 1000. What is its approximate ΔG′°?

options.text: −17.1 kJ/mol
options.why: ΔG′° = −2.303 RT log K′eq ≈ −5.7 kJ/mol × 3 = −17.1 kJ/mol.

options.text: +17.1 kJ/mol
options.why: K′eq > 1 gives a negative ΔG′°.

options.text: −5.7 kJ/mol
options.why: −5.7 kJ/mol corresponds to K′eq = 10.

options.text: −1000 kJ/mol
options.why: ΔG′° depends on the logarithm of K′eq, not on K′eq itself.

questions.outcome: Actual free energy in the cell
questions.stem: A step in a metabolic pathway has a positive ΔG′° but still runs forward in the cell. How is this possible?

options.text: The next step removes its product quickly, keeping Q small, so ΔG = ΔG′° + RT ln Q is negative
options.why: Direction is set by the actual ΔG, which depends on concentrations.

options.text: Enzymes change ΔG′° to a negative value by binding the substrate more tightly than the product
options.why: Enzymes never change ΔG′°.

options.text: ΔG′° has no relationship with reaction direction in any case, so its sign can simply be ignored
options.why: ΔG′° contributes to ΔG; it just isn't the whole story.

options.text: Cells run at a temperature close to 100 °C, which makes the TΔS term large enough to make it favourable
options.why: Cells operate near 37 °C.

questions.outcome: Actual free energy in the cell
questions.stem: ΔG′° of ATP hydrolysis is −30.5 kJ/mol, but in a red blood cell the actual ΔG is about −52 kJ/mol. Why is it more negative?

options.text: The cell keeps [ATP] far above, and [ADP][Pi] far below, equilibrium, so RT ln Q is strongly negative
options.why: Holding the reactant far from equilibrium makes ATP a more powerful energy source in vivo.

options.text: Red cells are about 100 °C hotter than 25 °C, so the TΔS term makes the hydrolysis more favourable
options.why: Body temperature (37 °C) changes RT only slightly.

options.text: Mg²⁺ is absent in red cells, so ATP is not stabilised as Mg-ATP and its hydrolysis releases more energy
options.why: Mg²⁺ is present; the true substrate is Mg–ATP.

options.text: The red cell's enzymes make ATP hydrolysis more favourable by lowering the activation energy
options.why: Enzymes affect rate, not ΔG.

questions.outcome: ATP, phosphoryl transfer and coupled reactions
questions.stem: Glucose + Pi → glucose 6-phosphate + H2O has ΔG′° = +13.8 kJ/mol, and ATP + H2O → ADP + Pi has ΔG′° = −30.5 kJ/mol. What is ΔG′° for the hexokinase reaction (ATP + glucose → ADP + glucose 6-phosphate)?

options.text: −16.7 kJ/mol
options.why: Standard free-energy changes are additive: 13.8 + (−30.5) = −16.7 kJ/mol.

options.text: +44.3 kJ/mol
options.why: This subtracts the wrong way; the values are simply added.

options.text: −44.3 kJ/mol
options.why: This treats +13.8 as −13.8.

options.text: +16.7 kJ/mol
options.why: The sign is wrong: ATP hydrolysis dominates.

questions.outcome: ATP, phosphoryl transfer and coupled reactions
questions.stem: Why is the hydrolysis of ATP to ADP + Pi so strongly exergonic?

options.text: Its products are more stable: charge repulsion is relieved and ADP and Pi are better solvated and stabilised
options.why: The free energy comes from the difference in stability between reactants and products.

options.text: Breaking the phosphoanhydride bond releases the energy stored inside the bond itself, as in a spring
options.why: A common misconception: breaking any bond requires energy. The 'high-energy bond' label describes the large ΔG of the whole reaction.

options.text: ATP hydrolysis has a very low activation energy, so the reaction releases its energy very quickly
options.why: ATP is kinetically stable in water; ΔG‡ affects rate, not how exergonic the reaction is.

options.text: Mg²⁺ is released as a gas when ATP is hydrolysed, carrying energy away from the reaction
options.why: Mg²⁺ stays in solution, bound to the phosphates.

questions.outcome: ATP, phosphoryl transfer and coupled reactions
questions.stem: Standard free energies of hydrolysis: PEP −61.9, 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate −49.3, phosphocreatine −43.0, ATP → ADP −30.5, glucose 6-phosphate −13.8 kJ/mol. Which compound CANNOT phosphorylate ADP to make ATP under standard conditions?

options.text: Glucose 6-phosphate
options.why: Its hydrolysis is less exergonic than ATP's, so transferring its phosphate to ADP would have a positive ΔG′°.

options.text: Phosphoenolpyruvate
options.why: PEP + ADP → pyruvate + ATP has ΔG′° ≈ −31.4 kJ/mol (pyruvate kinase).

options.text: 1,3-Bisphosphoglycerate
options.why: It makes ATP via phosphoglycerate kinase (ΔG′° ≈ −18.8 kJ/mol).

options.text: Phosphocreatine
options.why: Creatine kinase regenerates ATP from phosphocreatine in muscle.

questions.outcome: ATP, phosphoryl transfer and coupled reactions
questions.stem: Muscle cells contain high levels of phosphocreatine (about 28 mM in rat muscle). What is its role during a sudden sprint?

options.text: It rapidly regenerates ATP from ADP via creatine kinase, buffering ATP levels
options.why: With ΔG′° of hydrolysis −43 kJ/mol, phosphocreatine can transfer its phosphoryl group to ADP.

options.text: It is oxidised directly in the mitochondria to provide NADH for the respiratory chain
options.why: Phosphocreatine is a phosphoryl donor, not a fuel for oxidation.

options.text: It stores glucose units for glycolysis and releases them when the sprint begins
options.why: Glucose is stored as glycogen.

options.text: It inhibits ATP hydrolysis by myosin, so that the muscle's ATP lasts much longer
options.why: It replenishes ATP rather than blocking its use.

questions.stem: Glucose can be oxidised to CO2 and water by burning, or step by step through glycolysis and the citric acid cycle. How do the overall ΔG values compare?

options.text: They are identical: ΔG depends only on the initial and final states, not on the pathway
options.why: Free energy is a state function; the cell simply captures some of it as ATP instead of releasing it all as heat.

options.text: The cellular route releases more free energy, because each enzyme adds energy to its step
options.why: Enzymes add no energy to a reaction.

options.text: Burning releases more free energy because it is faster and runs at a higher temperature
options.why: Rate does not change ΔG.

options.text: The cellular route has a positive overall ΔG, because cells must invest ATP at the start
options.why: Complete oxidation is strongly exergonic by any route.

questions.outcome: ATP, phosphoryl transfer and coupled reactions
questions.stem: What is the true substrate for most ATP-dependent enzymes in the cell?

options.text: The Mg²⁺–ATP complex
options.why: Mg²⁺ shields the phosphate charges, and the ΔG of hydrolysis depends on [Mg²⁺].

options.text: Free ATP⁴⁻ with no bound metal
options.why: Most cellular ATP is complexed with Mg²⁺.

options.text: AMP
options.why: AMP has a single phosphate and is a product or regulator, not the energy donor.

options.text: Ca²⁺–ADP
options.why: Mg²⁺ (not Ca²⁺) is the relevant metal, and ADP is a product.

flashcards.back: 1st: energy is conserved (transformed, not created or destroyed). 2nd: the entropy of the universe always increases.

flashcards.front: Relationship between G, H and S?
flashcards.back: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. A negative ΔG means exergonic and spontaneous.

flashcards.outcome: Standard free energy and the equilibrium constant
flashcards.back: ΔG′° = −RT ln K′eq. K′eq > 1 → negative; = 1 → zero; < 1 → positive.

flashcards.outcome: Standard free energy and the equilibrium constant
flashcards.back: 25 °C (298 K), pH 7, all reactants and products at 1 M (gases at 1 atm).

flashcards.outcome: Actual free energy in the cell
flashcards.back: ΔG = ΔG′° + RT ln([products]/[reactants]). ΔG, not ΔG′°, decides direction.

flashcards.outcome: ATP, phosphoryl transfer and coupled reactions
flashcards.back: −30.5 kJ/mol (−7.3 kcal/mol). Actual ΔG in cells is about −50 to −65 kJ/mol.

flashcards.outcome: ATP, phosphoryl transfer and coupled reactions
flashcards.front: Why is ATP hydrolysis so favourable?
flashcards.back: Relief of charge repulsion, better solvation of the products, and resonance stabilisation of Pi.

flashcards.outcome: ATP, phosphoryl transfer and coupled reactions
flashcards.back: By coupling to an exergonic reaction through a common intermediate. ΔG′° values add up (e.g. hexokinase: +13.8 − 30.5 = −16.7 kJ/mol).

flashcards.outcome: ATP, phosphoryl transfer and coupled reactions
flashcards.front: Compounds with a higher phosphoryl-transfer potential than ATP?
flashcards.back: PEP (−61.9), 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (−49.3), phosphocreatine (−43.0 kJ/mol). These can make ATP from ADP.
A negative ΔG means a reaction CAN go; its rate depends on ΔG‡. Glucose + O2 is very favourable but slow without enzymes.
